Top state court nixes 10 Commandments monument at capitol

In 2005, in a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court determined that it was not a violation of the First Amendment to have the Ten Commandments at the state capitol. Here, we have a top state court saying it is unconstitutional under the state constitution.

If this case is appealed to the US Supreme Court, what are the possible outcomes?

Well I believe there were actually 2 rulings in 2005 on the same issue under difference circumstances. The one you mentioned is Van Orden v. Perry, there's also McCreary v ACLU. I only have a vague memory of either really, but it would seem context would be a determining factor. I believe the Van Order case largely hinged on having historical significance outside of a purely religious interpretation of value. In the current Oklahoma case the monument is only a few years old.

Wow, the "national cross" case. That one was just totally crazy! Oh, yeah, I remember that. That one bounced around for a while. There were actually two of those too, and one made it to the Supreme Court. Thanks for reminding me. I got hours of laughter out of that case as it was making its travels.

I'm not sure how the cross case is relevant to this Ten Commandments case.

In the Ten Commandments case, the state refused to remove the commandments from state grounds. The Supreme Court said they could keep it there for a number of reasons including

  1. It's not a religious symbol

  2. It's been there a long time

Here, we have the state saying it is unconstitutional. So this case flips the facts. May a state constitution prohibit the display? The state said yes.

This seems like a state issue to me, as it is "more protective" of separation of church and state than the feds would permit.

So, how would the Supreme Court justify this? The state can display its commandments but the state court can't interfere? That seems really strange. Maybe they just won't take the case.
